endpoints.notes: NEW. Self-service sign-up, unauthenticated (security: []). Body {email, password}; 'account name' is read as the email (Q1/A5), so SignInRequest/SignInResponse/POST /api/v1/sessions are untouched and the account signs in through the existing endpoint. 201 with {customerId, email, createdAt} and deliberately NO Location header and NO session token. 400 on a malformed address, a password outside 12..256, or an unknown property. 409 account_unavailable when the address is taken, decided by the lower(email) unique constraint rather than a pre-check so the concurrent case AC6 names resolves identically. 429 from the IP-keyed SIGN_UP bucket. No 401 (path is exempt from the session filter); no 503. GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE on this exact path must reach 405, not an unauthenticated handler.

NEW. Anonymous link creation, unauthenticated (security: []). Body carries longUrl only; alias and expiresAt are undeclared properties and answer 400 under the existing strict-body rule. 201 with {code, shortUrl, longUrl, createdAt, expiresAt} and no Location - status and clickCount are omitted because nobody may ever read them. Owner column is NULL, so GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/links/{code} answer 404 for every caller including the creator, and the code appears in no list. Expiry is app.links.anonymous-ttl (P30D) from creation, never caller-supplied. 422 url_rejected through the same validator and denylist as the authenticated path, including the new equivalent-form normalisation. 429 from the IP-keyed ANONYMOUS_CREATE bucket. 503 when the pre-issue cache invalidation cannot be done. No 401, by construction.

UNCHANGED by this design, and that is a deliberate constraint on it: AC5 requires a self-signed-up account to sign in here. 200 rather than 201 (no resource created). Unknown email and wrong password still give the same 401 invalid_credentials with the same timing. The one behavioural change is indirect and is a fix: after the lower(email) unique index, findByEmailIgnoreCase can no longer throw on a case-variant duplicate, closing a latent 500 on this frozen endpoint.

NARROWED, not edited. Same 201/400/401/409/422/429/503 shape as before. Host policy and the denylist now decide on the canonical host, so equivalent spellings of a refused host are refused: https://malware.example.com./x and http://2130706433/ move from 201 to 422. Forms java.net.URI cannot parse a host from (http://127.1/, http://0x7f.0.0.1/, unicode authorities) stay 400 - the 400-vs-422 split is unchanged (U1). No retroactive rescan (A4), so links already minted through those forms keep redirecting.

Unchanged. Owner-scoped in the query; anonymous links have no owner and therefore appear in no page, for any customer, ever. Regression surface for AC13 with NULL-owner rows now present in the table and in ix_links_owner_listing.
Unchanged. 404 now also covers 'created anonymously and therefore nobody's', byte-identical to 'never issued' and 'somebody else's'. Still never 403, still never 410.
Unchanged. An anonymous code answers 404 here for every caller: there is no way to extend or shorten an anonymous link's expiry, including by whoever created it.
Unchanged. An anonymous code answers 404. Nobody can take an anonymous link down through this route; the abuse-report path is the only takedown for one.

Unchanged, and unchanged on purpose (A15). Still 202 for any well-formed code including an anonymous one, and a report still blocks that link inside the 60-second bound. Carving anonymous codes out would reintroduce the existence oracle this endpoint's 202-for-everything exists to prevent, and an unowned link is the one most in need of a takedown path. Note the residual gap: abuse_reports.reporter_customer_id is NOT NULL, so only a signed-in caller can report an anonymous link.

Unchanged. 302 and never 301: a 301 is cached indefinitely by default, the second and later clicks never reach us, and the counts silently stop growing while a deleted link keeps redirecting from somebody's cache. An anonymously created code redirects through exactly this handler with the same Location, the same Cache-Control/Pragma/Expires and the same click counting (AC11) - the click path needs no edit, and an edit here would be out of remit.

Served by the same @GetMapping handler; Spring MVC dispatches HEAD to the GET mapping. Deliberately NOT a documented operation and it must NOT get its own annotation: the routes gate is a regex over @Get/@Post/... and a stray @RequestMapping in that file would be read as a path prefix. Listed here because the behaviour is real, not because a route is missing.

rationale:
WHAT IS FROZEN. artifacts/openapi.yaml at version 1.1.0 (7 paths, 10 operations, lint clean: unique operationIds, every operation has responses, all 20 local $refs resolve), 34 Java files under service/src/main/java, and service/pom.xml. `mvn clean -DskipTests compile` is BUILD SUCCESS on 65 sources. Five files are new (SignUpRequest, SignUpResponse, CreateAnonymousLinkRequest, AnonymousLinkResponse, HostNormalizer); the rest are edits to existing contract surfaces. service/pom.xml is byte-identical to what it was: nothing this change needs is a new dependency (@Email is in spring-boot-starter-validation, java.net.IDN is JDK), so this node does not force a supply-chain approval. The migrations will force one, from `implement`.

THE TWO BLOCKING AMBIGUITIES STILL CARRY NO HUMAN ANSWER, AND THIS CONTRACT COMMITS TO A READING OF BOTH. Q1 - "account name" is the email. Sign-up posts the same two fields sign-in posts; uniqueness is over lower(email); SignInRequest, SignInResponse and POST /api/v1/sessions do not move. The alternative is not a smaller change dressed differently: a separate username means a new customers column, a second sign-in identifier, an edit to a frozen request schema, and a ruling on which of the two identifies the seeded accounts under AC16. If a distinct username is really wanted, this must be said now - after `test-contract` it is a re-freeze, not an edit. Q2 - a duplicate sign-up is 409 account_unavailable, one new value in a catalogue this service documents as closed. AC6 requires the refusal to be visible, and there is no wording of a visible refusal that is not an account-existence oracle in a service that goes to deliberate lengths (identical 401s, timing-equalised sign-in, no 403, no 410) to avoid being one. So the decision was which status carries a disclosure that is inherent, not whether to disclose. The fallback Q2 offered - 400 invalid_request with fields.email - leaks exactly the same fact under a status that says the request was malformed, which it was not: it was well formed and lost a race, possibly by two years. The disclosure is bounded only by the IP-keyed sign-up bucket, which makes that bucket load-bearing rather than decorative; a reviewer who is unwilling to accept the oracle should reject this row rather than the bucket.

STATUS CODES, ONE AT A TIME. 201 on sign-up, because an addressable account is created - contrast POST /api/v1/sessions, which is 200 precisely because nothing is. No Location on that 201, and this is where I deviated from the clarification's proposed answer (Q7) on the strength of feasibility's U5: /api/v1/customers/{id} has no GET handler and sits inside the session filter, so it answers 401 without a token and 405 with one, for every caller including the account just created. Q9 used exactly that objection to strip Location from anonymous creation; taking it one way there and the other way here would be an inconsistency a client has to learn, and a Location that resolves for nobody is a promise that costs a breaking change to withdraw. The id is in the body, which is what a client actually needs. 409 for a duplicate account rather than 400, mirroring alias_unavailable: both are "you asked to create something under a name that is taken", which is what 409 Conflict means, and both refuse without naming who holds it. 201 on anonymous creation with no Location for the same reason as sign-up, plus a narrower body: no status and no clickCount, because AC13 says nobody may read an anonymous link's numbers and a body that carried them would invite a client to expect to fetch them later from an endpoint that will only ever answer 404. 400, not 422, when the anonymous body carries alias or expiresAt - those are unknown properties and the existing strict-body rule already answers 400 for unknown properties everywhere else; a separate request record is the mechanism, since reusing CreateLinkRequest would silently accept both. 422 url_rejected, not 400, for every host-policy refusal on both create paths, with one fixed message shared by denylist hits, internal hosts, our own origin and now un-canonicalisable hosts - a caller cannot tell from the wire which check fired, which is the intended trade and the reason the refusals are logged at INFO instead. A host that cannot be canonicalised fails closed to 422 and is never downgraded to 400 (A3): 400 would additionally tell a probing caller which spellings parse. 404 and never 410 for an expired anonymous link, and 404 and never 403 for reading one: 410 means "this existed" and would distinguish an expired anonymous code from an unissued one, handing an enumerator a free signal, and the whole architecture of AC13 is that unknown, expired, deleted, blocked, somebody else's and nobody's are one byte-identical answer. 302 and never 301 on the click path, unchanged and worth restating because an anonymous link now depends on it too: a 301 is cached by browsers and intermediaries indefinitely by default, so the second and later clicks never reach us - the counts silently stop growing, a deleted link keeps redirecting long after the 60-second bound, and none of it shows up in a test of our own service. 429 with Retry-After in whole seconds and never 0 on both new endpoints. 503 on anonymous creation but not on sign-up: 503 exists on the link create path because AC15 says degradation is spent on refusing new links rather than on serving clicks, and that sentence applies verbatim to the anonymous path; sign-up has no such dependency to shed and follows sign-in, which declares none. 405 - not 401 and not a handler - for GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE on the two newly exempted paths: shouldNotFilter is not method-aware, so an exempted path is outside authentication for every verb, and the only thing making that safe is that no handler exists for the other verbs. Not declared as operations, consistent with how 405 on /{code} is already handled.

THE NORMALISER IS THE DANGEROUS PART AND ITS SPEC IS IN THE SKELETON, NOT LEFT TO THE IMPLEMENTER. HostNormalizer.normalize(String) -> Optional<String>: empty means "cannot be canonicalised", which the caller must turn into 422 and must never fall back to the raw host. The javadoc fixes the exact steps and a worked table (2130706433, 0x7f000001, 017700000001, 0177.0.0.1 and 127.1 all to 127.0.0.1; MALWARE.Example.COM. to malware.example.com; 999.999.999.999 and 4294967296 and a..b to empty; 1.2.3.4.5 stays a name), because a blind test author writes HostNormalizerTest against this signature and AC1/AC2 assertions against these values. Two things a reviewer should check specifically. First, feasibility U2: the obvious implementation, InetAddress.getByName, is wrong on JDK 21 in the dangerous direction - it returns the public 177.0.0.1 for 0177.0.0.1 where curl reaches 127.0.0.1, and throws outright for 0x7f000001 and 017700000001. Built on it the fix would look complete with the loopback bypasses still open, so the four numeric forms are parsed by hand and only the resulting dotted quad is handed to InetAddress. Second, the over-normalisation risk that impact.json calls the single most dangerous failure here: normalisation never removes a label, so notmalware.example.com and malware.example.com.evil.test stay accepted while sub.campaign.malware.example.com stays refused, and no public host can be collapsed onto a denylisted parent or onto an internal address. The narrowing this causes on POST /api/v1/links is documented on the operation rather than mitigated: it is the requirement, there is no retroactive rescan (A4), and for a while the service refuses to mint URLs it is still serving.

UNKNOWNS I DESIGNED PAST, AND THE READING TAKEN. U1 (must forms java.net.URI cannot parse a host from become 422?) - no, they stay 400. They are already refused today, neither AC1 nor AC2 needs the change, and honouring it would mean moving host extraction ahead of parseOrThrow's null-host check, turning a documented 400 into a 422 on the exact split the existing suite pins. Normalisation therefore lands in requireShortenable and in DenylistThreatCheck, never in parseOrThrow, and UrlValidator's javadoc now says so where the implementer will read it. U2 (what "equivalent form" means numerically) - the browser/curl reading, hand-parsed, as above. U3 (does the live customers table already hold case-variant duplicates?) - unanswerable from this repository; only the two seeded rows exist here. It is not designed past so much as routed: the lower(email) index fails outright on apply if any exist, so note 7 in the contract requires the SELECT lower(email)...HAVING count(*)>1 result to be attached to the migration approval that Q11 already sends to a human. U4 (is 10/min the right anonymous default?) - I did not take Q4's literal 10. Q4's own stated criterion is "an order of magnitude under write-per-minute", and write-per-minute is 300, which yields 30; 10 is thirty times under. 30 also respects the documented house convention that production defaults are set so an ordinary integration test from one address never trips them - every test in this suite hits from 127.0.0.1 against a JVM-wide Redis that only some tests flush, and at 10/min the anonymous behaviour tests would cross-couple and fail for a reason that is not the code. AC14's property that actually matters (the anonymous route is never the cheaper way to mint links, and neither bucket can spend the other's tokens) holds at 30 with a 10x margin and holds mechanically, because Redis keys are namespaced ratelimit:<bucket>:<key>. An operator who wants 10 changes one number. U5 (Location on sign-up) - resolved by omitting it, as above. Q5 (trust X-Forwarded-For?) - no, unchanged: trusting a client-supplied header with no trusted-proxy list would make every IP-keyed bucket in the service spoofable, including the click and not-found buckets that already defend the redirect path. The consequence - behind a proxy that does not preserve the source address, every anonymous caller shares one bucket and 30/min is a global ceiling - is written into the contract and belongs in the runbook, not fixed in code.

WHAT THIS NODE DID NOT WRITE, AND WHY THAT IS NOT AN OMISSION. No controllers: routes are fixed by the spec and by the endpoints list, and the design node's remit is types and signatures. No migrations - service/src/main/resources/db/migration is outside this node's write paths, and both migrations are one-way in production terms, so they belong in the diff a human approves alongside `implement`'s code. Note 7 in the spec states them, their order (schema first, then rollout), and the duplicate check that has to precede one of them. No application.yml: every new property carries a @DefaultValue in AppProperties, so nothing must change there, and it is protected. No SignUpService, PublicLinkController or LinkService edits: those are T6/T13 and belong to `implement`. What I did add beyond pure DTOs, and why each was forced: RedisTokenBucketRateLimiter's capacityOf switch is exhaustive over RateLimitBucket, so adding two enum values without mapping them fails compilation - the two-line addition is the mechanical consequence of freezing the enum, not an implementation. LinkEntity's customer_id loses nullable=false (updatable=false stays, so a link can never gain or lose an owner) and CustomerEntity gains a public constructor, because "there is no constructor" was the previous contract and sign-up cannot be written against it. Four files got javadoc-only edits that delete claims this change makes false ("there is no registration endpoint" in SignInRequest and CustomerRepository) or pin where behaviour must land (UrlValidator, DenylistThreatCheck); leaving a frozen file asserting the opposite of the contract is worse than the diff noise.

RESIDUAL RISKS A REVIEWER SHOULD WEIGH RATHER THAN ASSUME AWAY. The rate limiter fails open when Redis is unreachable, so during a Redis outage both new unauthenticated endpoints are unmetered - including a 25.6 ms, 16 MiB Argon2id hash per sign-up. That is the existing, deliberate limiter behaviour and this change does not alter it, but it does put an unauthenticated database write and a memory-hard KDF behind it for the first time. Relaxing NOT NULL on links.customer_id is one-way: re-adding it later means deleting or re-homing every anonymous row, which is why the anonymous TTL is configurable and the rollback plan is "stop creating them and let 30 days drain". abuse_reports.reporter_customer_id stays NOT NULL, so only a signed-in caller can get an anonymous link taken down - the one link with no owner to complain about it. And during a rolling deploy the two new paths answer 401 or their documented status depending on which pod is hit; nothing in code fixes that, so they should be announced only after rollout completes.
